note:
Every magnitude constant that can refuse a practitioner's work, declared where it can be enumerated rather than met one at a time. The practitioner, 2026-10-22, after a week of them: "Where are these caps coming from? It seems from the outset of trying to use this widget there are caps left and right." and "I have wasted 2 days with these caps." Six fired in sequence over two days -- a graph-limit ceiling that equalled its own default, a pre-download count that counted ways and not elements, a junction cap derived from an isochrone measurement, a 30,000-vertex geometry cap, a 100,000-character provenance cap, and a 100 km edge cap -- and each was discovered only after the cost of the previous one had been paid. Blockers and directions have had a ledger, a clock and a validator since 2026-10-12. Caps had a prose inventory (experiment 125) that listed some of them and missed the rest.

Each cap here is also an individual in ontology/fieldwork.ttl, so a receipt can say which ones governed a run and at what value. A number that refuses work and cannot be queried is a number nobody can argue with.

basisVocabulary.measured: Taken from a measurement of the real thing, recorded with what was measured.
basisVocabulary.derived: Computed from a measurement, with any headroom stated.
basisVocabulary.undderived: Chosen. Says so, and carries a liftTest that would replace it with a measurement.

caps.evidence: localStorage accepted 5,226,496 bytes in both engines, probed 2026-10-19. docs/experiments/121-storage-beyond-local-storage.md.
caps.refuses: A workflow whose saved form does not fit the browser's small store.
caps.liftTest: Workflows move to the large store, at which point this governs nothing.

caps.evidence: One extent as JSON against the measured quota; about 26,000 vertices at the measured 39.2 bytes each.
caps.refuses: A single study-area outline too large to save.
caps.liftTest: The same as storage-quota: geometry leaves localStorage.

caps.evidence: Every extent one area has had, doubled by the two writes per save, leaving about 40% of the quota free.
caps.refuses: A study area whose revision history is too large to save.
caps.liftTest: The same as storage-quota.

caps.evidence: Bunia normalizes to 42,796 junctions and Buvuma Island to 11,359, measured 2026-10-20; the default must not refuse a town.
caps.refuses: Nothing by itself. It is the default value of a knob a practitioner sets.
caps.liftTest: Not a cap to lift: a default to re-derive when a larger real area is measured.

caps.evidence: Chosen 2026-10-21 to sit past what a public Overpass instance will serve in one request. It was 50,000 -- the default itself -- so the knob could be lowered and never raised, and the byte cap derived from it could never be raised either. That is the cap that cost two days.
caps.refuses: A graph limit a practitioner tries to set above it.
caps.liftTest: A measured response size at which a browser actually fails, replacing a chosen number with a met one.

caps.evidence: 270 and 272 bytes per junction measured on two extents 2026-10-13, carried at roughly double as headroom. A province measured 163 on 2026-10-21, so the padding is nearly fourfold at that scale.
caps.refuses: Nothing directly; it sizes the download byte cap from the graph limit.
caps.liftTest: Re-derive from province-scale measurements rather than neighbourhood ones.

caps.evidence: 1.42 MB over 9,458 elements is 150 B; 7.39 MB over 50,791 is 145 B. Unpadded, because it predicts a response rather than bounding one.
caps.refuses: A download whose predicted size, from the service's own count, exceeds the byte cap.
caps.liftTest: Nothing to lift: it is a measurement used to refuse before bytes are spent, which is the cheap place to refuse.

caps.evidence: 1.80 and 1.87 features per junction measured 2026-10-13, carried at roughly double.
caps.refuses: Nothing directly; it sizes the feature cap from the graph limit.
caps.liftTest: Re-derive at province scale.

caps.evidence: 2.19 measured on real street data (11,497 over 5,249); 2.04 measured on a province 2026-10-21.
caps.refuses: Nothing now. It sized a graph refusal that was removed on 2026-10-21.
caps.liftTest: Not a cap any more; kept because the pair is still reported.

caps.evidence: Twice the largest extent this project had measured (7.39 MB), so the floor cannot refuse an example it ships.
caps.refuses: Nothing: it is a floor under the byte cap, not a ceiling over it.
caps.liftTest: Not applicable.

caps.evidence: Twice the 50,791 features of that same extent.
caps.refuses: Nothing: a floor.
caps.liftTest: Not applicable.

caps.evidence: Raised from 100,000 on 2026-10-22, when 2 of 314,955 segments in a province's driving network were over it, the longest 100,723 m. A collapsed chain between junctions in rural Ituri is genuinely that long. 1,000 km is kept as a unit check: a length in degrees, or kilometres read as metres, lands orders of magnitude away.
caps.refuses: A single street segment longer than 1,000 km.
caps.liftTest: A unit declared on the field, at which point the magnitude check has nothing left to catch.

caps.evidence: A 1 km square of central London normalizes to 5,249 junctions and exhausted a 4 GB heap during isochrone construction, 2026-10-13. The threshold sits below what failed.
caps.refuses: Nothing. Above it the isochrone step warns, and its own worker timeout reports what happened.
caps.liftTest: An isochrone implementation measured past it -- the street engine drew one over 1,152,974 junctions in 0.14 s on 2026-10-22, in WebAssembly and not in this code.

caps.evidence: A 292-pixel Inspector figure. A province's 3,755,832 segments would be tens of megabytes of path data and thousands of strokes per pixel.
caps.refuses: Nothing. Beyond it the picture is an even sample and the caption says so.
caps.liftTest: Not applicable: a limit on a drawing, not on data.

caps.evidence: Measured 2026-10-22 on the Ituri extract in the Inspector: 113,485 nodes and 289,080 directed edges serialise to 41.8 MB pretty-printed and 59.7 MB after escaping, about 203 MB of UTF-16 held per render, in a collapsed <details> that showed none of it. Chrome killed the renderer. 20,000 elements is about 1.9 MB, the limit this same control already states for upload.
caps.refuses: Nothing about the network. Above it the hand-edit textarea is not offered and the panel says so; the file input stays and the graph is still held, drawn, run and exported.
caps.liftTest: Not applicable: a limit on a text box, not on data.

caps.evidence: The largest graph this project has downloaded from the service, parsed and drawn: 27,181 junctions from a 7.39 MB response, 2026-10-13.
caps.refuses: Nothing. Above it the download warns that nothing larger has been tried.
caps.liftTest: A larger response downloaded, parsed and drawn, which replaces the figure.

caps.evidence: A province's driving network read from a 416 MB published extract and taken into this application's structures, 2026-10-22. Held, not yet drawn, routed over or snapped to.
caps.refuses: Nothing. It is what the extract control reports having been measured to.
caps.liftTest: A larger extract-built graph drawn and routed over, which replaces the figure.

caps.evidence: Chosen so buffering many geometries yields to the event loop rather than blocking it. No measurement recorded.
caps.refuses: Nothing. It is a batch size, and a smaller one is only slower.
caps.liftTest: A measurement of frame time against batch size, which would replace the choice with a number.

caps.evidence: The Inspector panel is 292 pixels wide; the figure is that less its padding.
caps.refuses: Nothing. It is the width of a drawing.
caps.liftTest: Not applicable: a panel dimension, not a limit on data.

caps.evidence: Two thirds of the figure's width, so a square extent is not stretched.
caps.refuses: Nothing. It is the height of a drawing.
caps.liftTest: Not applicable: a panel dimension, not a limit on data.

caps.evidence: How finely a partial edge's corridor is approximated. Measured 2026-10-14 against an exact construction: 161,044 m2 against 160,785, a symmetric difference of 0.16%, and not purely conservative -- which the code states rather than assumes.
caps.refuses: Nothing. It trades area accuracy for work, and the error is measured.
caps.liftTest: Not applicable: an approximation parameter with its error stated, not a limit on data.

caps.evidence: A RESPONSE budget, and only that since 2026-10-22. Raised 2026-10-19 from 20,000 after a one-line probe to overpass-api.de took 14.2, 27.3 and 26.3 seconds while answering 200 every time -- which showed 20 seconds was too short and nothing more. The replacement was borrowed from OSMnx, where 180 seconds is passed to Python requests, and there it is not a limit on a download at all: requests raises only when no bytes have arrived for that long. Imported here as a total elapsed deadline it meant something else, and aborted a transfer that was working.
caps.refuses: A service that has not begun to answer within three minutes. It no longer refuses a transfer that is arriving; STALL_MS governs that, which is what the borrowed number always meant.
caps.liftTest: A measured time at which a response of a given size actually arrives, so the budget follows the size rather than a borrowed default.

caps.evidence: When the panel says in so many words that the service has gone quiet. It was 180,000 -- inherited from the response budget it replaced -- which meant a stalled transfer showed its last byte count for three minutes and looked exactly like one still arriving. Ninety seconds is the practitioner's, 2026-10-22: "180s may be too long to wait to say it's stalled. 90s, time to give feedback." The faster half of the feedback is the transfer rate, said every second, which falls on its own the moment chunks stop.
caps.refuses: Nothing. It is when a sentence appears. A download that has begun to arrive is ended only by the practitioner pressing Stop.
caps.liftTest: Not applicable: a threshold for a status line, not a limit on data.

caps.evidence: How much history the transfer rate is averaged over, so the number is not noise between chunks and still falls while someone is watching it. The practitioner, 2026-10-22: "Feedback could also be bytes/sec download speed. If the user sees it going down, that's immediate feedback."
caps.refuses: Nothing. It is the width of an average shown in a status line.
caps.liftTest: Not applicable: a display window, not a limit on data.

caps.evidence: Five minutes across the probe, the count, the failover attempts and any wait for a free slot. It is consulted between attempts and to bound a wait, never during a transfer: a stream that is delivering is governed by STALL_MS alone.
caps.refuses: A download whose attempts together run past five minutes before a service begins to answer.
caps.liftTest: The same measurement: a budget derived from response size rather than chosen.

caps.evidence: How long this client waits for an instance's /api/status before calling it unreachable for the purposes of choosing one. Chosen.
caps.refuses: Nothing a practitioner asked for: a slow status read only removes an instance from the preference order.
caps.liftTest: Not applicable: it bounds this client's own impatience, not what can be found.

kindVocabulary.artefact: Bounds something this application makes and controls: a 292-pixel drawing, a batch size, how finely a shape is approximated. Reasonable by construction -- the thing it bounds is ours, and the practitioner loses nothing they came to find.
kindVocabulary.platform: A limit the environment imposes, which this application measures and reports rather than chooses. The remedy is to name it, never to pretend it is not there.
kindVocabulary.discovery: Bounds what a practitioner can find out. These are the dangerous ones. The practitioner, 2026-10-22: "There are reasonable caps and unreasonable ones... The others are unreasonable because they are imposing limits on things we have yet and need to discover (the DE angle)." A number chosen here decides the answer to a question nobody has asked yet.

ceilingRule: It may be lowered freely and may never be raised. Widened 2026-10-22 from chosen numbers alone to every discovery cap whose basis is not a measurement. The practitioner, on finding a borrowed 180 seconds stopping a working download: "That is the definition of an unreasonable cap, which I thought we know how to classify already." The classification was right -- attempt-seconds was declared discovery, derived, with a liftTest naming the measurement that would replace it -- and it bound nothing, because only undderived caps were counted. A derived number is still a number nobody measured here.
